v.why: With e3 removed the output relies on edges 4 and 5 only, so deleting edge 5 removes a much larger share of the signal (e.g. #80 IN16 -18.9).
If edge 5 is already absent, deleting edge 4 leaves the output fed only by edge 3, which hurts more (e.g. #36).
When edge 4 is missing, edge 3 is one of only two inputs to the output, so removing it hurts much more (e.g. #11 IN16 -15.5).
Replacing a missing edge 0 restores node 1's only input and all routes through it, which is a much larger gain than swapping one existing op for another (#85).
Reconnecting node 1 when edge 0 was none brings back edges 2 and 4, while replacing a conv on edge 0 with skip removes capacity (#92 vs #1, #15).
Without the direct input-to-output edge, the route through edges 2 and 5 carries more of the signal, so cutting edge 2 hurts more (#95).
When edge 0 is none, edge 1 is node 2's only input, so turning it into a parameter-free pool degrades the main route (#71 C10 -20.5).
Replacing a convolution on edge 5 with skip removes learnable capacity, while replacing none or a pool with skip is neutral or helpful (#90, #100).
Swapping the strongest op, conv3x3, for average pooling on an output edge causes a large drop (#50 -12 to -16), bigger than replacing skip or none.
Adding a conv3x3 where the direct input-to-output edge was absent adds both a new route and capacity, so the gain should exceed that of replacing an existing op on edge 3.

Ten hypotheses below. They rest on one structural reading of the cell plus the 100 measured edits. The reading: node 3 (output) gets its inputs from edges 3, 4 and 5. An edit hurts or helps much more when the parent leaves only one working route to the output, or when it touches an edge that is the only way into an intermediate node.

| # | Edit | Condition | Direction | Main supporting experiments |
|---|------|-----------|-----------|-----------------------------|
| 1 | edge 5 → none | e3 = none | lower | #80: IN16 −18.9 |
| 2 | edge 4 → none | e5 = none | lower | #36: −2.1 / −5.3 / −5.6 |
| 3 | edge 3 → none | e4 = none | lower | #11: IN16 −15.5 |
| 4 | edge 0 → nor_conv_1x1 | e0 = none | higher | #85: +75.7 / +61.1 / +31.2 |
| 5 | edge 0 → skip_connect | e0 = none | higher | #92: +13 to +20 |
| 6 | edge 2 → none | e3 = none | lower | #95: −4.1 / −4.7 / −9.9 |
| 7 | edge 1 → avg_pool_3x3 | e0 = none | lower | #71: C10 −20.5 |
| 8 | edge 5 → skip_connect | e5 = nor_conv_1x1 | lower | #90, #100 |
| 9 | edge 4 → avg_pool_3x3 | e4 = nor_conv_3x3 | lower | #50: −12.3 / −16.4 / −10.2 |
| 10 | edge 3 → nor_conv_3x3 | e3 = none | higher | #77, no direct contrast |

**How strong the evidence is:**
- Most of these rest on only one or two experiments that meet the condition. Each edit-and-condition pair appears only a few times in the 100 experiments.
- Hypotheses 4, 5 and 7 have no measured contrast at all. Edge 0 → skip_connect (#1, #15) is the only one of the three with measurements on the non-matching side. All of the non-matching cases there have e0 = nor_conv, never avg_pool_3x3.
- Hypothesis 10 is a prior more than a result. #6 shows a larger gain when replacing nor_conv_1x1, but in that parent edges 4 and 5 are both none, which confounds it.
